in writing. the gradual liberalisation of visa requirements with a view to visa-free travel is one of the main tools for bringing the peoples of the european union and the eastern partnership closer together. since the first prague summit in 2009, most partners have made significant progress in implementing the reforms required by the european union. the republic of moldova has succeeded in lifting the visa requirement as early as april 2014. the eastern partnership summit in riga is expected to decide on the prospects for visa-free travel with further countries, georgia and ukraine, and visa facilitation with belarus. the issue of visa liberalisation is of political, social and economic importance and its acceleration is therefore a key element in shaping the bilateral relationship. visa-free travel is an opportunity to strengthen cooperation between the eu and the eastern partnership countries; half a million moldovan citizens benefited from it in its first year. open borders are of great importance not only for trade, culture and social exchange, but also for the democratic aspirations and the aspirations to freedom on which the idea of a common europe is based. the difficult reforms facing our eastern partners are expected by the people of the eastern partnership countries and the eu as they have an impact on enhancing security in the region. we hope that as of 2016, citizens of georgia and ukraine will benefit from the right to visa-free travel.
president-in-office of the council.– madam president, let me use this opportunity to signal once again the high political importance of the youth employment initiative and to thank parliament for the very fruitful cooperation that allowed us to react promptly to the challenge of youth unemployment. members have asked what is holding member states back. at this point in time, it is still difficult to fully assess the actual progress on the ground, as the reporting cycle at eu level has not yet started. aside from the financial liquidity issue, which is the most pressing one, i could refer to three other challenges to the sufficiently speedy mobilisation and uptake of youth employment initiative measures: firstly, some member states lack the implementing structures; secondly, there is the matter of finalising the designation of competent authorities, which has also been emphasised by some member states; and, thirdly, there are a number of issues related to the administrative capacity of the national, regional and local structures implementing youth employment initiative measures. so how does the council intend to urgently encourage swift and efficient implementation? the council considers, in line with the european parliament, that sufficient liquidity will also allow for a faster implementation of the relevant policy measures set out in the national youth guarantee implementation plans. the new proposal to increase pre-financing should contribute to a quicker mobilisation of resources and thus to increasing the capacity of national authorities to launch calls for projects and to process applications more speedily. the additional pre-financing will be paid to member states immediately after the entry into force of the amending regulation. a positive impact could be expected soon. on the other hand, the implementation of the youth guarantee requires both structural reforms and measures targeting individuals. member states are currently implementing a mix of national youth employment policies on the basis of their individual needs and priorities, with the youth guarantee scheme representing one of these measures. all relevant member states have submitted their youth guarantee implementation plans and the implementation at national level is being regularly monitored by the council, based on contributions from the committee on employment and social affairs in a multilateral and indicator-based process. exchange of experience between member states is also important, as well as impact evaluation of the measures carried out. to conclude, i would like to underline that member states are currently in the process of submitting structured data reports on the implementation of the youth employment initiative. these reports will provide an overview, also limited, of the progress made by member states in the implementation of the youth employment initiative, which will feed into the commission’s analysis of further measures and into the regular monitoring by the council. effective monitoring is thus one of the preconditions of successful implementation and continuity of sound funding. in this respect the council, on the basis of the work of the committee on employment and social affairs, is pursuing a multilateral surveillance on implementation and undertaking a peer review on the progress in the implementation of the reforms addressed in the country-specific recommendations. last but not least, based on the experience of 2014 and with little improvement of the youth employment figures in some of the hardest-hit member states, it can be expected that this issue will be addressed in the framework of the 2015 european semester debate. in any case, the council will discuss this issue in more detail at the june session in conjunction with a special report of the court of auditors. member states will also have to further strengthen their efforts, focus on implementing relevant structural reforms and deliver quality measures to enable young people to participate in the labour market, training or education. these will also be very important measures. to sum up, the council shares the view that more needs to be done to fight youth unemployment. i have just mentioned a few examples of measures underway in the council and the commission with the aim to make the system more effective. i cannot promise members a miracle solution tomorrow, but i can firmly say that hard work is being done to find a solution as soon as possible.
in writing. i think that in her question, ms ulvskog has raised an important point. i would point out that the problem of not using the funds sufficiently or quickly enough is not just a problem of the youth guarantee but also of cohesion policy funds in general. so we need to consider what causes it and what we can do about it. i believe that the best way to increase and accelerate the absorption of funds is to simplify procedures as much as possible. in addition, additional support from the commission, both information and technical, which could facilitate the collection and use of funds by member states and beneficiaries, should be considered. it should be borne in mind that the youth guarantee is a unique aid measure designed to bring about a rapid improvement in the dramatic situation on the labour market. i therefore call on the commission to be flexible and proactive in its action.

president-in-office of the council.– madam president, i would like to thank you for this very important and very lively debate. as i have already mentioned in my opening remarks, cyber-attacks, including those targeting media, are an increasingly worrying trend. the growing sophistication of cyber-attacks and cyber threats around the world, and their use as an element of hybrid warfare and terrorist attacks, oblige us to stand on high alert and continue working to improve our capabilities to tackle this threat. we should continue to invest our efforts in guaranteeing the implementation of the existing tools and the full use of the eu initiatives dedicated to the fight against cyber threats. we should also continue and intensify work to provide for new and more comprehensive responses to the constantly evolving challenges posed by this threat. the council remains fully committed to work constructively towards the adoption and effective implementation of concrete measures in that respect. mr schwab and some other honourable members have reminded us of the importance of reaching an agreement on the directive on network and information security. today the presidency and the european parliament received key input from the commission on its recommendations for the most challenging issues in the directive, regarding its scope and several aspects of implementation, that will be instrumental in making the last remaining strides towards a compromise between the council and parliament. with this directive the eu is going into unchartered territory in attempting to make our new digital lives more safe and secure. this is, admittedly, not an easy process, as developing legislation on a highly technical issue that touches at the same time on national security is no easy task. the latvian presidency continues and will continue to work to make significant progress on this issue by the end of june. we are confident that the good spirit of cooperation which prevails will allow us to reach a timely conclusion of the negotiations on the directive on network and information security in order to provide the eu and its member states with an instrument to improve its preparedness and capabilities for action in case of cyber-attacks. at the same time, regulation of such innovative sectors must be achieved in a prudent and balanced manner in order to avoid placing an unnecessary burden on an industry that is creating growth and jobs. we shall also continue our efforts towards introducing effective and creative practical, preventive and control measures that will go beyond the necessary legislative minimum. strategic communication, countering propaganda, and international cooperation are on our list of priorities. at the same time, despite this late hour, i would like to recall the root cause of such attacks targeting independent and professional media. dramatic changes in the media landscape, in particular the introduction of new technologies, have resulted in an unprecedented flow of information. despite draconian measures, neither totalitarian regimes nor terrorists are able to firmly close the tap and fully prevent the information flow. journalists’ independent voices and reports give the international community a unique insight into realities on the ground, including in conflict zones. it is thanks to journalists’ courage that the world is aware of what happened in chernobyl, chechnya, libya, rwanda and srebrenica and what is happening in north korea, afghanistan, iraq, syria and ukraine. the media serve as a catalyst for a rapid and effective global response, and thus they are vital to the survival of a democratic society. it is for this reason that all of our activities aimed at improving security, resilience and capabilities should go hand-in-hand with activities aimed at safeguarding and reinforcing the ability of the media to provide independent and reliable information.
in writing. ladies and gentlemen, cyberattacks on the media are a new threat to cybersecurity, as they are aimed at generating terror and thus threaten one of the basic institutions of democracy. these attacks reveal the brutal truth that no one is safe today. they demonstrate that terrorism and cybercrime can generate catastrophic consequences that directly affect citizens. at any given moment, the internet is spreading about 150,000 viruses that infect the hardware and software of over 1 million users every day. the recent attacks on french tv channel tv5 monde and belgian daily le soir only confirm concerns about the ease with which cyberattacks are being carried out. we live in a digital age today, where virtual reality is no less real than the real world. for this reason, cyber attacks must be seen as as dangerous as attacks on physical structures. the european commission and the member states should adopt swift solutions to improve cybersecurity at european level. this means better cooperation between national and european institutions, in line with real efforts to combat such threats together. concrete solutions and a clear presentation of the current state of cybersecurity are needed.
in writing. it is naive to think that we will be able to bring about rapid improvements in internet security and safety in the near future. while we observe and respect the efforts being made, we must accept that cyberattacks will be repeated, perhaps intensified. in my view, the attempt to create a single centre to counter these types of threats is a road to nowhere. without the far-reaching efforts of all stakeholders, no cyber-attack response project can succeed. it should be noted that too often we neglect the individual security of users and their data. we have a huge gap in education about how to use the internet safely in a way that protects your data and makes using the internet completely friendly. we should not just focus on the emergency firefighting, but address the problem from the bottom up, teaching and spreading good practices in using the network. finally, i would like to mention that the internet is also a giant business and that the owners of large internet companies also have a huge responsibility to protect, especially those youngest users, from abuse online.

in writing. one of the objectives of the post-2015 development agenda is to strengthen the rights and empowerment of women and girls. achieving this priority requires stepping up action to eliminate harmful practices that violate women's rights, such as early, forced marriage, which affects 14 million girls a year. forced marriage is an extreme form of violence against women and a major obstacle to the achievement of gender equality. the european parliament, in its 2006 resolution on women's immigration: the role and place of women migrants in the european union, stressed that 'violations of human rights, including the rights of girls, in the form of forced marriages or other violations cannot be justified by any cultural or religious considerations and should under no circumstances be tolerated'. issues related to women's rights, including forced marriages, must be addressed in the context of bilateral association agreements and other agreements with third countries. education and awareness-raising programmes focusing on forced and arranged marriages are also key. finally, it is essential that all states accede to the convention on preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence, so as to establish a common policy of protection and international cooperation for the protection of women's rights.
in writing. early marriage and forced marriage continue to be widespread in the world. despite international commitments, this problem significantly limits human rights, especially for women and children, and hinders development and poverty reduction. the eu's human rights strategy 2012-2014 identified the prevention of child marriage as a priority for the member states and the european external action service. this important commitment was reiterated in the eu action plan on human rights and democracy 2015-2019, which includes the targeting of child, early and forced marriages. i support the european parliament's strong position on combating all forms of discrimination and violence against women, including forced marriages.

in writing. ‒ i strongly support the continuation and expansion of the programmes for the supply of fruit and vegetables, bananas and milk to educational establishments, which play an important role in promoting healthy eating habits and the consumption of agricultural products in the european union. i also agree with the need to expand the range of dairy products so that children with lactose intolerance can also benefit from the programme. it is important that the regions, which are best aware of the needs and capabilities of local educational establishments, are involved in the development of programmes and in the decision-making on the products to be distributed in schools, in addition to the member states. i also pay particular attention to the educational activities that accompany the distribution of agricultural products to schools. knowledge of healthy eating habits, agriculture, and environmental protection is crucial to shaping the quality of life and health of children and young people. developing the habit of eating fruits and vegetables among young people is the best investment in their health and well-being. remember, children are learning from their parents, who can also play a very important role in this program by encouraging their children to eat vegetables. in order for children in each member state to benefit from this programme, it is also important to take responsibility for its financing, which means increasing its budget so that it also covers dairy products.
over a month ago, ireland held a constitutional referendum on a different but similar issue, which introduced a new definition of family into the constitution. well, this referendum raises fundamental doubts about the course of its campaign. in our letter to the president we wrote that the question of funding was raised. the fact that the state-funded parties threatened to exclude politicians who were involved on the side of the minority in the referendum.
fundamental democratic principles have been violated, including above all the principle of the first minority, which is the party that is in the minority in the public debate but should have the same rights. therefore, i am requesting that this matter be discussed, the conduct of the referendum: whether both parties had the guaranteed guaranteed in irish law right of equality in the public debate.
the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. we are discussing today the adoption of a position on the correction coefficient for direct payments for calendar year 2015. this is the so-called financial discipline mechanism, which was provided for in the horizontal regulation of december 2013 as part of the latest reform of the common agricultural policy. the main objective of the fund is to establish a crisis reserve to support the agricultural sector in the event of major crises affecting agricultural production or the distribution of agricultural products. the total amount of the contingency reserve for the period 2014-2020 is set at eur 2,8 billion, which is equivalent to eur 400 million per year in 2011 prices. the application of financial discipline to direct payments in 2015 is part of the preparation of the union budget for 2016, in which the commission has set aside eur 441,6 million in current prices in the crisis reserve. after preliminary estimates for direct payments and agricultural market expenditure, the european commission assumed that an adjustment of less than 1.4% for direct payments would be sufficient. it should be stressed here that this deduction will only apply to farmers receiving more than eur 2000 in payments per year. in addition, due to the full payment inquiry in bulgaria, croatia and romania, financial discipline will not apply to these countries. according to the regulation, the correction coefficient should be adopted by co-decision of the council and the parliament by 30 june. therefore, as soon as we received a request from the european commission, our committee on agriculture in parliament decided to apply the simplified and accelerated procedure provided for in rule 50 of the rules of procedure, according to which i, as chairman of the committee responsible, drew up the draft report without amendments after my report had been adopted without amendments in the committee on agriculture and no amendments had been tabled for this plenary session. i hope that in tomorrow's vote we will finally be able to accept the european commission's proposal without amendments. with a clear declaration from the council, which also confirmed in writing its willingness to accept the commission's proposal without amendments, this will mean that we will be able to reach an agreement at first reading within the time limit set by the regulation. the recent disturbances on european agricultural markets, due to the russian embargo and the expiry of milk quotas, show the importance of this reserve. its importance is further enhanced by the reduction in intervention mechanisms that has taken place in the context of the recent reform of the common agricultural policy, or by the increasing influence of external factors such as the progressive liberalisation of world trade in the context of the profitability of european agriculture and european farmers. i don't think anyone in this room needs to be convinced that agriculture is a very sensitive sector, heavily dependent on weather, climate, the price situation in world markets, speculation or international events. in view of the controversy over the agricultural budget last year, i would therefore like to stress that the agricultural appropriations which are returned to the agricultural budget should remain there to be used to combat the effects of the crisis. i would like to emphasize that this reserve is created from the funds that are in the common agricultural policy, the farmers are freezing them as it were. we're taking a portion of the payments to make a contingency reserve. if this reserve is not used, then these funds go back to the farmers, so you can say that the farmers create a reserve for themselves.
on behalf of the ecr group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i am speaking on behalf of the epp group on the regulation of the parliament and the council fixing the correction coefficient for direct payments for the calendar year 2015 to be paid in the financial year 2016, and i would like to say that my political group supports this solution and will vote in favour of it. the establishment of that coefficient, as well as the emergency reserve in the financial year 2016 of eur 441,6 million in current prices, means that this reserve can be used for agricultural emergencies. it should be noted that it will consist of direct payments above eur 2000 per holding and will also not cover the three countries where payments are incomplete, namely bulgaria, romania and croatia. although the creation of the correction coefficient and the emergency reserve means a corresponding reduction in the national direct payment envelopes for individual eu countries, the creation of this reserve in such uncertain agricultural management conditions is, in our opinion, appropriate and necessary. the eu is also facing a number of challenges, including the continuing russian embargo on food products from eu countries, the deterioration of the situation on many agricultural markets, including the milk market, falling purchase prices for many agricultural products and the opening of eu markets to food imports from third countries through the reduction of eu customs duties. all of this only increases the risk and uncertainty of agricultural production. i would therefore like to express the hope that the crisis reserve will be used in 2016 to support those farmers and agricultural markets where the situation will be most difficult.
mr. chairman, please! solidarity is a great european value: the principle that one for all, all for one. in the name of solidarity, sanctions were imposed on trade with russia, because that is what the security of europe requires, because that is what it requires to stand firm against russian expansion, a threat to peace in europe. on the other hand, this principle of solidarity has not worked or has worked very poorly, because it is the farmers who have suffered the economic consequences of these sanctions. the farmer in finland, the baltic states and poland, the farmers who could not sell their milk or their apples (in the case of poland, this was a real tragedy, because a million tonnes of apples had been sent to russia and this was stopped), the farmers in other countries, france and germany, also suffered great losses - they suffered losses of several billion euros, and the aid that the farmers received was only hundreds of millions of euros, and it was not even fair, not always distributed reasonably. it is a pity that this fund, which is set up every year in the event of a crisis and is quite substantial, has not been used for this purpose. the question is, what is the purpose of this fund if it hasn't been used in a situation like the russian embargo? i urge you to use this fund wisely in future and to use it in such situations.
member of the commission.– mr president, i want to thank all of the members who contributed to this debate, and in particular i would like to thank mr siekierski, the rapporteur, for bringing forward this report tonight. i want to commend the last common agricultural policy reform, and the people associated with approving it, for providing a crisis reserve without requiring additional finance to be provided for agriculture. this, in essence, shows the solidarity of the european union with the farming community at times of crisis. i welcome the support shown here today for the proposal which will establish this reserve for 2015 for the benefit of farmers in particular difficulties. the crisis reserve is solidarity in action. after all, as i said, it is funded from the existing resources of the farming community. many members raised the russian ban and its consequences for european farmers. i want to remind you that, last october, the commission had a proposal which would have utilised the crisis reserve of eur 433 million for that particular foreign policy decision. in november the new commission was in a position to reverse that decision and to provide from other sources the resources necessary to show solidarity with the farming community at times of difficulty, arising from the russian ban. if fully drawn down, these measures will cost eur 350 million, without reference to the crisis reserve. members like mr dantin who made considerable representations on these matters will, of course, recall these particular measures very well. but i know that many members have forgotten these particular decisions that were made in november in order to counter the concerns of many members of the committee on agriculture and rural development (agri) at that time. i wish to thank budget commissioner georgieva for being very sympathetic to providing that positive outcome for european farmers at a difficult time. i would say to ms schreijer-pierik, in relation to pigmeat, that i opened aids to private storage in order to recognise the difficulties for pigmeat producers in many member states. this scheme was open for about 10 weeks. it provided a withdrawal from the market of a significant tonnage from the pigmeat sector, and it has certainly stabilised incomes for many pigmeat producers. i also provided an opportunity for additional promotion measures for the pigmeat sector to replace some of the market share that was going to russia, particularly in countries like the philippines in the far east, which now account for 73% of the products in the pigmeat sector that had been going to russia. so the market-orientated policy that you have voted for and supported is working in action in relation to how we are dealing with the pigmeat sector. in terms of the application of financial discipline adjustment, it is important to remind ourselves that small farmers throughout the eu are exempted by the application of the eur 2000 threshold, below which the adjustment rate does not apply. i know that when mr ashworth said earlier that, because of their farm structure, a lot of farmers in the uk – and indeed in other member states – would not have to pay this particular contribution, he was certainly reflecting the reality of the fact that larger and medium-sized producers are the ones in a better position to pay for this particular instrument. mr agnew made another very valuable contribution with regard to the uk staying in europe, because he will know better than anybody that looking for eur 25 billion – which is the amount of money that the european union is subsidising british farmers at the moment – will be very difficult when you are competing with the public services around the cabinet table of a uk government. the eu is quite generous to british farmers – and rightly so – in addition to all of the other farmers in the union. i would subscribe to the view that the eu will always be more supportive of agriculture and rural development measures in the uk than its own government is. i want to conclude by repeating my welcome for the proposal, and i look forward to a positive vote tomorrow.
the rapporteur. this report is formal and technical in nature, and the discussion was very substantive, which i would like to emphasise and for which i would like to thank you. the accelerated procedure for adopting this document means that there is a high degree of agreement between the council, parliament and the commission, which is worth emphasising in these responses to needs or difficult situations. it was about solidarity, because almost everyone, except the smallest, is in fact eligible for aid, and it is farmers who are affected by a difficult crisis situation who benefit from this aid. so this solidarity is extremely important. let's remember that agriculture has its own specificity: it depends on climatic conditions, weather, external conditions. at the moment, the dependence on the international situation is also very clear. this requires certain instruments which the free market is not always able to generate. the free market requires some support to counteract these agricultural emergencies. we should also remember that the major weakness of the reform of the common agricultural policy which we are currently implementing is precisely the limitation of forms of intervention on agricultural markets. i've talked about the purpose of these interventions, and in that limitation, we've gone too far. that's why good market management is important, because we have less money at the moment for the cap in general, less money for agriculture-related things. i think we cannot say that the cap is leading to a crisis. the cap supports agriculture and also supports consumers because this support for agriculture makes food cheaper and consumers pay less for the products they buy. i would like to thank the presidency and the commission once again for their cooperation.
in writing. agriculture, as one of the most vulnerable sectors of the economy, requires special protection. the establishment of a contingency reserve of eur 441.6 million is of the utmost importance for the protection of the interests of farmers in the eu. the current geopolitical situation in europe and the resulting breakdown in agricultural markets have exposed the imperfections of the current crisis response legislation. the introduction of the russian embargo on eu agricultural products, the continuing fall in the purchase prices of agricultural products, and the opening of eu markets to food imports from third countries through reductions in eu customs duties all point to increasing risks and uncertainties in the agricultural sector. i believe that the report of the committee on agriculture on the correction coefficient for direct payments for 2015 should be accepted, as the creation of a crisis reserve in a period of destabilisation of the european agricultural economy is absolutely necessary. the reserve is intended to protect european agriculture and give the european farmer a sense of at least relative security.
in writing. the correction coefficient for direct payments for 2015 concerns the establishment of a reserve to support the agricultural sector in crisis situations, and these funds are obtained through a reduction in direct payments, but only among those farmers who receive support above eur 2000 (except for farmers from croatia, romania and bulgaria, who have not yet reached the 100% ceiling for subsidies). the correction coefficient is 1,39%, which will provide a reserve of eur 446,1 million in the 2016 budget. it is worth noting that if the funds mentioned above are not used, the money is returned to the farmers the following year. we are all well aware of the fragility of agriculture and how easily the market can be disrupted, leading to surpluses or huge losses, which drastically reduce farmers' incomes. this is influenced not only by weather conditions and climate change, but also by the political situation in europe and beyond (the latest examples being the olive oil epidemic, the milk sector disruption and the effects of the russian embargo). the crisis reserve is therefore an absolute necessity, a mechanism to guarantee the smooth functioning of european agriculture, which i fully support.
draftsman of the opinion of the committee on employment and social affairs. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i would like to highlight in today's debate the theme of the importance of gender equality for the competitiveness and growth of the european union economy. gender equality in the labour market is undoubtedly a matter of social justice, a fundamental civil right, but it is also a prerequisite for sustained and sustainable economic growth. the full use of women's skills, education and talents brings real benefits to businesses and economies. the presence of women on boards, the presence of women in positions, is tied to the profits of the company. the 39% pension gap in europe is a great shame, this pension gap should be the first starting point and reference point for building equality policies, and we know well that to do this we need nurseries, kindergartens, care services and the possibility of reconciling work and family life.
on behalf of the ecr group. we are discussing a controversial and threatening report today which is supposed to be a coherent and effective strategy for gender equality. such an ideal strategy should be a field of cooperation between women and men and be based on access to equal opportunities in a way that respects and values the natural differences between them. but the report we're discussing has nothing to do with the actual idea of equality. it promotes abortion as one of the reproductive rights, intervenes in education by introducing a gender perspective at every level of education, calls for the adoption of a directive establishing gender parity in company supervisory boards, violates the natural identity of the family by promoting parenthood for lgbt people, and also points to the obligation to combat stereotypes and traditional perceptions of the roles of women and men, and demands the involvement of the commission and the member states in the in vitro procedure. the report entries interfere with the competence of the member states and are not in accordance with national rules. this report is a collection of different solutions, good and bad, but unfortunately, the bad ones will open the door to social dismantling and to the undermining of the institution of the family. it's these threats that are the essence of it. the report must not be allowed to pass, and that is why i will support amendment no 1 in tomorrow's vote, which respects the division of powers between the union and the member states and takes account of the rules of international and eu law on health and family policy. let us not allow the idea of equality between women and men to be the sole and exclusive field of unnecessary ideological struggle. the question of the equality of men before the law and of men before each other is one of the most important civilizational challenges facing mankind. the european union has a leading role to play in achieving this humanitarian objective. at the same time, however, we must tackle the inequalities that exist within the member states themselves. this also applies to inequalities and even discrimination against women. so, first of all, i think that we can't deal with all the different kinds of inequalities between women and men without strengthening education. education and training should therefore be the most powerful tools to combat prejudice, stereotypes and the consequences of viewing the issue through the lens of misconceived tradition or religion. secondly, the most important challenge is faced by politicians. because if conservative forces block civilization change, we're not going to achieve optimal outcomes for gender equality, especially in the short term. so politicians, especially in the individual member states, must take the responsibility for this on their own shoulders. the third and final issue in this synthesis speech the area where radical change is needed is the labour market: employment, including women's wages, and flexible working hours. there will be no equality if women cannot achieve the same level of self-fulfillment in the 21st century society as men. so i think the strategy for gender equality that i've been discussing in most of my writing is very much relevant to the challenges that i've been outlining. answer the question asked by raising the blue card. i believe that education should be understood and treated broadly in this context. it is not just about education for children and young people, although i am convinced and i know from experience that in many member states of the european union we do not have a good enough level of education. but this education must not be limited to children and youth. it must be applied to all societies, regardless of age, because these very stereotypes, those inherited from the past and tradition, and sometimes unfortunately also from religion, have and are ingrained in people of different ages.
i would like to draw the attention of the european commission to the very difficult situation of farmers - milk producers - in my country, poland. as a result of the russian embargo, as well as the lifting of the milk production limits, the prices of this raw material have already fallen by about 20%. at the same time, farmers will be charged with penalties for exceeding production limits for the second year in a row. the fines will amount to around €150 million and will be levied on farmers' payments for ongoing milk deliveries until september this year, with prices for the raw material delivered to the buying points falling sharply. in this situation, after the fines have been paid, the remaining part of the milk sales revenue is certainly not sufficient to cover the production costs, which means losses and the inability to settle the remaining liabilities of the dairy farms, including credit liabilities. i therefore ask the commission once again to take an interest in the situation of dairy farms in poland and to prepare solutions to support dairy production throughout the union in this very difficult period for milk producers.

in writing. enforcement of intellectual property rights (ipr) is the basis for employment growth and development in the union and for the proper functioning of the single market and of the many industries benefiting from such rights. it is also a major catalyst for innovation, creativity and competitiveness. as the european commission points out, high-iqm sectors account for around 39% of eu gdp, or approximately €4.7 billion per year, and provide up to 35% of all jobs. i therefore welcome the eu action plan on ipr enforcement, in particular the focus on targeted information campaigns and the enforcement of rights through a 'follow the money' approach, ensuring that those who commit serious ipr abuse and profit from this illegal practice are punished. however, the commission's ipr enforcement efforts will need to be adapted to the development of the digital single market, which is becoming the main trading venue for counterfeit goods. in this context, online platform owners should be involved in enforcement issues and in efforts to exclude those responsible for infringements in online trade in goods. it should be borne in mind that the trade in counterfeit products not only causes loss of income for businesses and the european economy, leading to job losses, but also poses a threat to the health and safety of consumers.

in writing. ‒ the creation of a crisis reserve for the agricultural sector is a necessary financial instrument. in poland, where agriculture is still a significant part of the economy, we have been watching with great concern the struggles of farmers who have tried in vain to find new markets for their products after the russian embargo. i voted in favour of the report on the correction coefficient for direct payments for 2015 because i fully support the rights of farmers in the european union and consider the right to protect their work and property to be one of the most important. i think that the solution adopted in the report by the committee on agriculture, which allows farmers to receive at least partial compensation in the event of a natural disaster or economic crisis, is a good one. the lessons of the past year have taught us that having a financial reserve to draw on in times of crisis is a prerequisite for ensuring stability and further development of the european agricultural economy.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report setting a correction coefficient for direct payments. i also congratulate the rapporteur, mr ašersky, on his work on this document. i think that additional support for the agricultural sector is particularly important at the moment. the sanctions imposed by russia on the european union have particularly affected european agriculture. the losses of polish farmers alone due to the export ban to russia amount to $500 million. i therefore believe that the inclusion of the proposed amount of eur 441.6 million as a reserve for the crisis in the agricultural sector is right and proper.
in writing. ‒ due to technical problems, i was unable to vote on this report. however, as rapporteur i naturally support it and my intention was to vote in favour of its adoption. the financial discipline mechanism under the cap is a good example of solidarity, as direct payments to farmers for 2015 will be reduced by 1,45 to create a crisis reserve in 2016. this reserve has not been used until now because there was a free budget in the cap for crisis management, which meant that the money went back to the farmers the following year.

in writing. ‒ the report on the eu strategy for equality between women and men after 2015 has generated a lot of controversy, including on the subsidiarity principle. this non-legislative document has above all a political value, setting the standard and direction for equality policies in europe. i think the most important chapters are those on women in the labour market, which talk about the need to reduce the employment, wage and pension gaps, which in europe are 11%, 17% and 39% respectively. as a result, women are poorer than men and more likely to be victims of domestic and sexual violence. economic independence and equal opportunities in access to the labour market, including senior positions, are important tenets of this report. on the issues of differentiating positions within the group, i voted for the maternity directive, quotas on company boards, the anti-violence directive and the european observatory on violence, incentives for paternity and parental leave, easier access to in vitro, quotas on electoral rolls, access to reproductive health and rights services, reproductive health education and incentives for research and gender studies. as in the previous report on this subject, i was against the paragraphs on increasing access to abortion for social reasons.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the eu strategy for equality between women and men after 2015. in the context of this report, i would like to draw attention again to the issue of maternity leave and the importance of education in promoting gender equality, combating violence and promoting equal work for equal pay. in today's highly competitive job market, many women are afraid to become mothers for fear of losing their jobs. it is therefore essential to ensure that they are protected also after the end of the maternity period and to guarantee social protection for women who, due to the nature of their employment relationship (service contract), do not benefit from maternity leave at all. we cannot tackle the ageing population unless we take action to stimulate demographic growth by protecting women's rights. in the context of educational activities, we need elements of equality policy in educational programmes to teach young people mutual respect, tolerance and to fight against various types of prejudice and stereotypes. social campaigns that draw attention to relevant issues, mobilize action and promote certain norms, behaviours and values also play an important role in this regard.

in writing. ‒ the eu strategy for equality between women and men for the period after 2015, adopted by the european parliament, is a very damaging and dangerous document. first of all, the very fact that it's there is a misunderstanding. it not only interferes with the exclusive competence of the member states to decide on worldview issues, but also defines social problems in a wrong way, full of ideological prejudices and simplifications. secondly, it presents socially harmful phenomena such as abortion and gender ideology in a one-sided and biased way, and it refers in a critical and inconsistent way to the social roles of women and men, the traditional model of the family and the right of every human being to life from the moment of conception. this strategy is an example of very damaging social engineering and the negative impact of the radical voice of homosexual and far-left communities on the european political class - a voice that europe should not listen to under any circumstances if it wants to face the social and demographic crisis that affects it. i hope we can keep this worldview madness going. i voted against the document, of course.

madam president! i would like to start by making it clear that i consider the extension of the kyoto protocol to be an important step in the fight for a better climate for our planet. however, i share the rapporteur's concern that the efforts to reduce emissions are being made mainly by european countries, while the most polluting countries do not seem to be as determined. in march, the union's position was set for the forthcoming climate summit in paris. a very ambitious position, talking about even more reductions after 2020. i believe that a realistic, broad international agreement based on voluntary action is better than the imposition of specific binding targets, which we decide to adopt only in the context of the 28 member states. at the same time, i believe that it is clear that the obligations of individual countries should vary, since the poorest countries are not in a position to meet such ambitious standards. i think it's time that the major polluting countries also made a greater effort and signed a joint international agreement.
member of the commission. madam president, i am pleased to take part in this debate on the european energy security strategy. i would like to extend my sincere thanks to all the honourable members who will be taking part in it, but i am especially grateful to mr saudargas and all the rapporteurs for the efforts they have made to produce this balanced report from the european parliament on a subject which is very topical, but at the same time very sensitive. i would also like to thank you for the excellent cooperation you have maintained with the commission throughout this process, providing us with many opportunities to share and explain our views. the draft report before us is an excellent result of the work and commitment to energy security, which is in addition to the political impetus we have wanted to give to this and other matters with the energy union. let me explain why we think this is an important report. firstly, because it maintains and reinforces a balanced and comprehensive approach to energy security. energy security is a very complex issue requiring action in different policy areas and at various levels of decision-making. we need to maintain this balanced approach if we are to successfully tackle this collective challenge. in this sense, the draft report reflecting the structure of the energy security strategy of may 2014 seeks to respond not only to our short-term challenges, however politically sensitive they may be, but looks beyond them, taking into account strategic priorities, both within and outside the european union. in this broad concept of energy security, the achievement of a genuine internal energy market is fundamental, as are research and innovation. i would like to congratulate myself on the fact that the draft report we are discussing today has placed particular emphasis on the need to moderate energy demand and increase domestic production, mainly from renewable energy sources. the commission fully shares this approach. we will continue to build on this strong political message from parliament, especially in the context of the next cop 21 conference later this year, with the aim of achieving a historic agreement to combat climate change. at the same time, this draft report, in its external dimension, mentions the most urgent supply problems we face and highlights very clearly the dependence on a single supplier for energy resources, with the resulting vulnerability and lack of competition, because it can impede economic growth and endanger the national security of the european union. the commission shares this view. so, we're going to work to diversify our sources and supply routes. to this end, we will continue to work on the southern gas corridor, the mediterranean and algeria, as well as relations with our traditional partners such as norway, the united states and canada. i have already visited several of these countries in recent months, aware that a diversification of routes and suppliers is fundamental for the european union. in northern europe, the establishment of liquefied gas hubs, with multiple suppliers, is greatly improving security of supply, and this example should be followed in central and eastern europe and the mediterranean area. in this regard, we are preparing a liquefied natural gas and storage strategy to be adopted later this year, together with the revision of the regulation on the security of gas supply, two key pieces for diversifying supply and being prepared in the event of gas supply disruptions. i was also pleased to note that the report again stresses the need to speak with one voice on the international scene and calls on the commission to develop a proposal for mandatory ex ante evaluations of intergovernmental agreements with regard to their impact on the internal energy market and their compatibility with european union law. i can assure you that the commission is working on this and plans to present a proposal in the first half of 2016. finally, i would like to stress the emphasis the draft report places on the energy union strategy, adopted by the commission in february this year. as you know, energy security is one of the three overarching objectives of the commission's energy union strategy. our energy must be secure, competitive and sustainable. of course, the three objectives are interdependent and go hand in hand. the implementation of the european energy security strategy has therefore been fully integrated as a core element of the energy union strategy. we are planning to publish the first report on the implementation of the key actions related to the european energy security strategy at the end of this year and i am confident that dialogue in the european parliament will be, throughout the process, a key pillar of our action.

madam president! the european energy security strategy is the next stage in the construction of the energy union. the completion of this project is the foundation of the european union today. among the many important demands for the energy efficiency of the internal market and the increase of domestic energy production, special attention should be paid to conventional and non-conventional energy sources within the european union. no discrimination can be allowed between any of the energy sources. i would like to draw particular attention to the increasingly clean and efficient technologies for coal combustion and shale gas production. these are the two most important factors in ensuring energy independence in europe based on indigenous resources and have a major impact on energy prices, especially electricity prices, which are among the highest in the world in the european union.
the advantage of the european energy security strategy is that it recognises the need to diversify energy supplies and sources. it is also important that it strengthens regional cooperation in the field of energy. these are very important postulates. but we cannot be uncritical of this document. i personally am very strongly opposed to the decarbonization postulate. for countries like poland, decarbonising the economy means the collapse of many jobs and the increase in energy poverty. the disregard for this problem undermines the idea of european union solidarity and the sincerity of the intentions in building a strong european union economy. you say that countries like poland have to adapt and have to give up fossil fuels. you say these words and demands lightly and without deep reflection. you don't care what it costs my country and a few other countries. you don't care who pays for it. do you know that meeting these demands will mean the loss of 500,000 jobs in my country over the next decade? who will compensate, and how? it's easy to talk about decarbonization to you, the rich countries, whose economies have been unfettered by any such restrictions for decades and have been growing unfettered. ladies and gentlemen, the final sentence of the president, an energy-safe european union is one that respects the interests of all its members, not just the strongest players. i ask you to remember that. i hope my foreword will return to health and strength. to return to the subject, the european energy security strategy should be one of the community's most important documents. it is concerned with ensuring a good future, development and relative independence from energy or energy sources outside the territory of the member states. a document of this kind should therefore be narrowed down to the strategically necessary priorities. the energy union and the policies of the member states should play a part in this. one of the main pillars of this strategy should be the strong involvement of indigenous energy sources, which are the key to external independence. the commission therefore concludes that the aid is compatible with the internal market. emphasis should also be placed on supporting research and development of modern clean technologies from indigenous sources. unfortunately, the strategy under discussion does not in principle provide for such assumptions, on the contrary. for these reasons, it is more an ideological position than a substantive one. for these reasons, it is a document that, i'm sorry to say, will be difficult to accept.

madam president! i think that no one in this room needs to be convinced of the enormous importance of the european union's energy security and of the impact it has on our position, on the political and economic position of europe, especially in the context of the crises that are at european borders. i believe that the european union should step up its efforts to diversify its energy supply, because we cannot rely on a single source, which comes from a country as insecure as russia, a country that is clearly challenging eu rules and using energy for political purposes. but there is another aspect to this: i believe that energy security, the security of the european union, cannot be based solely on renewable energy and be identified with it. i think we should do everything we can to make the use of energy sources such as shale gas available in european countries, which i am convinced will help to increase the diversification and increase the security of the european union countries in terms of energy.
energy security, or more broadly, the energy union, is already a permanent part of the european union's vocabulary. the battle of words has been won. no wonder, since we are under the influence of such an important geopolitical lesson as the one provided by modern ukraine. the previous disruptions to the gas supply were not enough to teach a lesson. that lesson is enough, but if we don't question the goals, then our collective responsibility is implementation, so that energy security doesn't share the fate of all those declarations that remain declarations. as usual, the most difficult challenge is to balance the eu's climate and energy agenda. i believe that the original report by deputy saudargas is on that track. it also follows our efforts, which i remember from the end of the barroso commission, and which resulted in the proposal to bring together the climate and energy agendas, as happened in the case of commissioner cañete. if this balance is not achieved, it is difficult to achieve other objectives: competitiveness, security, reindustrialisation, and it is bad if the union declares objectives and fails to achieve them. what is striking in these documents is the poorly defined, timidly defined external aspect of the coordination of eu policies towards the main suppliers. but i also see amendments that are unbalancing the climate and energy agenda and therefore don't seem to deserve support.
madam president! the energy union is intended to be a consensus between climate priorities and a strategy for security of energy supply, low prices and competitiveness. this will be achieved through strategic investments on the one hand and increased energy efficiency and the share of renewable energy on the other. the current efficiency directive is flawed because it presupposes the same reduction in energy use in eu countries with different energy use. the efficiency ratio as a policy objective for member states should take into account the gdp per capita of those countries. the aim of the new directive cannot be to reduce energy use but to increase its physical efficiency as the main method of decarbonisation. in the diverse economies of eu countries, which differ greatly in energy consumption, the lack of a way of calculating this target - different for whole countries and different for industrial sectors - does not stimulate innovation in both efficiency and renewable energy investments. the commission considers that the aid is compatible with the internal market if it is granted to a company that is not subject to the obligation to provide the relevant information to the commission.
madam president, first of all i would like to congratulate mr saudargas on his report and thank him for the hard work he has done. i fully support many points included in the report. for example, the rapporteur correctly emphasises the need to reduce the eu’s dependence on foreign energy sources, including russian oil and gas, and to establish an energy union in europe. nevertheless, the current version of the text is, in my opinion, not as good as the original draft. the main weakness of the document is that it is one-sided and focused excessively on environmental and climate aspects of energy policy at the cost of energy security as such. a good illustration of these biased proportions is that the word ‘renewable’ appears 74 times in the text of the report, while the word ‘competitiveness’ only appears 10 times. clearly, the issue of the impact of the energy security strategy on the growth and competitiveness of european companies is not given sufficient attention. another weakness of the report is that it largely ignores the potential role of some indigenous sources of energy such as clean coal and shale gas. in particular, the issue of clean coal has not been discussed at all, which i found very surprising. the report is very optimistic on the issue of expanding energy generation from renewables. however, there is no solid evidence that a massive and rapid shift from fossil fuels to renewables is indeed technologically feasible and economically viable in the foreseeable future. i hope, commissioner, that these points will be taken into consideration.
in writing. energy security is undoubtedly a pillar of the energy union. recent events in eastern ukraine, as well as the european commission's stress tests last year, have clearly demonstrated the dangers of energy dependence. i believe that the european union should therefore make it a priority to diversify gas supplies and to reduce its dependence on third countries. i am glad that mr saudargas has made this clear in his report and that he has called for the acceleration of the diversification of suppliers, routes and sources of energy, which i believe is the right thing to do. i also think it is extremely important that the european union, as a powerful market and one of the world's largest energy markets, should speak with one voice on key issues such as the turkish stream project.
in writing. given that energy security is closely linked to political independence, the eu should work towards a common and effective energy security strategy. it should be remembered that the eu still imports as much as 53% of its energy and many member states are dependent on a single external source. in addition, a significant proportion of energy imports come from politically unstable regions, which significantly increases the threat to energy security. the eu should therefore work together to create an internal energy market, develop energy technologies and diversify energy supplies. however, the european energy strategy should build on the diversity of member states' energy resources. the new criteria for a low-carbon, renewable energy economy must take into account the situation of countries that rely on coal for energy production. the new strategy cannot be implemented at the expense of those countries whose primary energy source is coal. we all agree that we need a coherent and long-term energy strategy, but it must be based on fair conditions.
in writing. the eu's approach to energy security is changing to its benefit. in recent years, it has become clear that the level of this security is fundamental to europe's standing, its economy and the lives of its citizens. it is worth remembering that 53% of total energy consumption in the union is still covered by imported energy and many member states are dependent on a single external supplier. the european parliament should therefore strongly support the european commission's efforts to not only increase security of supply but also to move towards the european energy union. the basis for such a union should be close coordination of the energy policies of the individual countries and the presentation of a common position in contacts with suppliers.

in writing. ‒ the need to increase the union's energy security has been discussed for many years. progress has certainly been made, but much remains to be done. the very fact that there is still not enough transmission infrastructure between member states and that there are therefore so-called energy islands shows how grossly neglected we are. how can we talk about the energy security of the union if there is no interconnected area in practice? so it seems to me that this is the direction that we should be going in first. if we make the union an energy area, we can more easily deepen our cooperation, whether through the creation of an energy union or through the creation of real solidarity mechanisms. unfortunately, i was eventually forced to vote against the report on the strategy for energy security because of the very unfavourable provisions on coal mining, shale gas or the use of nuclear energy. i believe that only by making intelligent use of our natural resources will europe be able to ensure its energy security. therefore, support for sources such as coal and shale gas is necessary.
in writing. ‒ the current geopolitical situation is forcing the eu to step up its efforts to create a self-sufficient energy market and to provide energy security for europe's citizens. more than half of the energy consumed in europe today comes from imports, and many member states obtain their energy from a single source or from a single external supplier. meanwhile, the crisis in ukraine and russia's behavior have shown how unreliable a partner it is and how much it can flout our rules. it is necessary to find new sources of energy and new, stable suppliers, and and perhaps above all to develop the internal energy market. the energy security strategy must be a long-term strategy, taking into account a wide range of aspects, such as increasing local energy production and rational distribution, technological development and upgrading of existing production units, innovation in renewable energy and social campaigns to encourage sustainable, energy-efficient management. we must also not forget the potential of the agricultural sector in this area. biofuel production must be an important part of the energy strategy. the european union's proper energy policy is one in which we remember solidarity and mutual trust; one in which we stand united and present a common position in negotiations with third countries.
in writing. ‒ to ensure energy security, we need to focus on renewable energy, promote energy efficiency and invest the money we spend on expensive imported fuel in developing our green technology industry and creating new jobs.
in writing. ‒ a key priority in the implementation of the european energy security strategy must be to ensure that no country in the union is left without excessive interruptions in energy supplies from a single supplier. this requires, among other things, diversifying supply sources, creating more connections between member states and modernising existing transmission networks. in poland, a significant part of the power plant and transmission networks is outdated, decapitalised and inefficient. the poor state of the technical infrastructure is a very serious threat to energy security. i also draw attention to the question of energy prices. ensuring an adequate level of energy security in the eu should take into account the guarantee of affordable energy prices for all eu citizens. for example, given the differences in purchasing power between eu countries, poles pay some of the highest energy prices. in addition, one in four union citizens was affected by energy poverty in 2012. citizens must also be adequately informed about energy prices, opportunities to improve energy efficiency and reduce energy consumption.
in writing. ‒ as co-rapporteur for the epp group on the report on the european energy security strategy, i have spent the last months working hard on this document so that it can be approved by the european parliament. unfortunately, his final version was unacceptable, so i voted against it. the document put to the vote, although it contains many positive solutions, such as strengthening the internal energy market, calling for greater coordination in the choice of energy suppliers between member states and reducing the eu's dependence on a single supplier, as a whole fails to achieve its objective of increasing energy security for the european union and its member states. it should be stressed that the european energy security strategy is a document of particular importance and as such should be formulated on the basis of strictly defined priorities. however, the final version of the treaty became an ideological manifesto: if implemented, many of its provisions would firstly jeopardise the economic and therefore social development of the european union and secondly would not guarantee the energy security that europe so badly needs.

the president-in-office of the council. - madam president, i have to go. i'm not going to let you down. ladies and gentlemen of the house of commons! first of all, thank you for inviting me to speak on this important issue of transparency in the application of the stability and growth pact. the stability and growth pact is central to the work of the european union. it constitutes a rules-based framework that contributes to sound budgetary policies and the sustainability of public finances across the european union. these provisions leave the european commission and the council with a sufficiently wide margin of manoeuvre in assessing the budgets of the member states and allow them to take account of the specific circumstances of each country, so that reliable, independent and reliable assessments of the economic situation play an essential role in the functioning of the system. these important aspects are also mentioned in the report on economic governance by mrs berès, which we have just discussed. in this context, i would like to highlight the substantial improvements introduced in economic policy coordination in recent years. i think it is safe to say that the new institutional structure laid down in the pact strengthens the commission's role and right of initiative. the new rules also increase the accountability of member states and the transparency of the process. all the documents relating to the process are publicly available on the european commission's website, and the new approach also allows for a more robust and broader assessment of the different economic factors involved in the member states and the european union as a whole. the council bases its discussions on an independent analysis of the economic situation prepared by the european commission, as presented, for example, in the staff working papers and forecasts. we also use information provided to the council by the member states concerned, in particular on new or additional discretionary policy measures, where they implement such measures. the member states' positions are then discussed and finally agreed with the aim of achieving the desired result, a stable and sustainable fiscal position. the same approach was also used in assessing the situation and deciding on the excessive application of the budgetary procedure to france. ladies and gentlemen of the house of commons! the three priorities of this year's economic policy coordination cycle, or european semester, are to: first, boost investment; second, implement structural reforms; and third, develop a responsible fiscal policy. in other words, while fiscal responsibility is of immense importance, it is only one of the necessary elements. the importance of structural reforms and investment alongside a responsible fiscal policy is also underlined in the commission communication on the application of the principle of flexibility in the stability and growth pact. the council has exchanged views on this communication and found a consensus that the flexibilities provided for in the existing rules should be used. the council continues to work towards a common understanding of the application of the principle of flexibility. finally, i would like to say a few words about the importance of the stability and growth pact in the wider context, and its role in the development of european economic and monetary union. on 24 october 2014, the european summit gave the task of preparing the next steps for better economic governance of the euro area, and on 22 june 2014 the five presidents' report on the completion of european economic and monetary union was published. it proposes a gradual approach to strengthening european economic and monetary union in the short term and to perfecting the structure of european economic and monetary union in the long term. the european council of tomorrow is scheduled to hold a first exchange of views on the report of the five presidents, and the council stands ready to work constructively on the issues outlined in the report in all appropriate formats. as i mentioned in the debate on the preparations for the european council today, it is essential to make every effort to promote convergence, as the current divergence between euro area member states could jeopardise the future of the union as a whole. we are ready to work constructively to implement the proposals contained in the report, and the council of europe's guidelines will play a key role in this process. ladies and gentlemen of the house of commons! i really believe that we will be able to achieve a common vision for the future of european economic and monetary union and we will be able to implement it. thank you for your attention.
vice-president of the commission.– madam president, honourable members, the commission shares parliament’s concern about transparency and the implementation of budgetary surveillance and agrees on the need for scrutiny on the part of the main stakeholders and of the public in general. certainly things can be improved upon. but let me start by illustrating what is already in place. i will start by talking about transparency and then move to the scrutiny part. as you know, the work of budgetary surveillance by the commission is based on its economic and fiscal forecasts. the commission provides and publishes regular country-specific aa, ea and eu-level analysis of the economic perspectives. in addition the commission produces, once a year, country reports that contain a comprehensive analysis of the economic situation, including in-depth reviews under the macroeconomic imbalances procedure, where relevant, and an assessment of the main challenges. concerning, in particular, fiscal surveillance, the assessments of the commission are accompanied by detailed technical analysis prepared by the services, which are also made public. all the relevant results and documents are publicly available on the commission’s website. thus, all the elements needed to perform the commission’s analysis and calculations are publicly available. we can certainly further improve and facilitate access to this amount of information, and i thank you for having brought the issue to our attention. in this connection i am glad to announce that we are planning a new version of a public commission staff document on the rules of the stability and growth package, the so-called vademecum. in this document we will clarify even more the methodology that we use to assess whether the member states, under the excessive deficit procedure, have taken the action required by the council.this is the technical component of the analysis, which has then to be validated by the college. at the moment, all results and methodologies, including detailed information, top-down and bottom-up approaches, can be found in the relevant documents available on the commission’s website. but we are aware of the need for further clarification and we will act decisively in this sense. when we are looking at commission decision-making, the judgements and decisions taken by the college are certainly political, but they are based on independent analysis of the relevant facts and the applicable rules. in this respect the commission cannot change the 3% deficit rule and the 60% debt rule of the stability and growth pact, which are enshrined in the treaty, of which the commission remains the guardian. the commission document on flexibility is just an interpretative communication which provides additional guidance for the implementation of the stability and growth pact, without ordering the rules themselves. indeed, due to the complexity of the facts to be determined and of the economic analysis to be performed, the sgp provisions leave a substantial margin of appreciation to the commission and to the council. with the aim of providing transparency and predictability, it is therefore in the commission’s remit to provide further interpretation of the stability and growth pact provisions without changing or replacing them. rules for sound public finances, of which the stability and growth pact is an expression, are necessary for the existence of the monetary union and, more in general, for sustainable growth. they are even more important now that growth is coming back and we need to avoid repeating past errors. the commission improved the surveillance cycle by presenting the economic analysis in country reports three months earlier than in the past. the commission is also currently engaging in a dialogue with the european parliament and the council in the context of the so-called two- and six-pack review, and five presidents, including the european parliament president, are discussing the future of emu, including its governance mechanism. honourable members, as a conclusion, the commission is committed to improving the surveillance framework. our desire is to take this way all together.
on behalf of the ppe group.– madam president, the stability and growth pact is an important instrument for ensuring fiscal discipline in the member states. however, this whole discussion this evening demonstrates that neither members of this house, nor the member states in particular, are very happy with its application. i am very happy to hear commissioner katainen promise to improve the transparency and efficiency of the stability and growth pact. one way, or one avenue, to improve the situation would perhaps be to consider adding to the existing main measure of fiscal discipline – which is, of course, the deficit – some other measures, such as for instance debt-to-gdp ratio. the deficit measure, be it in the form of a headline deficit or a structural deficit, suffers from important weaknesses. one of them is that the deficit gives us a short-term picture of the budgetary situation and actually is not a good measure of long-term sustainability in terms of fiscal policy. the other thing is that the deficit is very much dependent on cyclical factors, ad hoc measures and also discretionary policy measures taken by individual governments. the structural deficit is mostly a variable which is not directly observable and is also dependent on the potential output, which is again a concept that is difficult to measure and difficult to present in a convincing way. so maybe one possibility of improving the situation would be simply to shift to the debt-to-gdp ratio. this would give you at least a long-term measure of fiscal sustainability.
in writing. the stability and growth pact is an important instrument for ensuring fiscal discipline in the member states. in 2011, thanks to the hard work of the european parliament and the european commission, the pact was significantly deepened. the commission took on a particularly heavy responsibility then and now is the time to remind it of that. the commission must play the role of independent budgetary controller if our economic and monetary union is to be credible in the future. ensuring the stability and sustainability of the european economic system is necessary and urgent to get back on the path of growth and jobs. the rules of the stability pact should apply equally in all countries. the independent economic assessment must be transparent and effective, and i welcome the assurances given by commissioner katainen. we need to ensure that budgetary policies are responsible and that our financial markets converge. it is also important to strengthen political legitimacy, which is why parliament should be more involved. what methods does the european commission use to carry out analyses of the economic framework? what methodology does the commission intend to use to assess the budgetary position of a member state and its structural budget surplus and to estimate potential gdp growth? these are questions that the european commission should answer first.
